## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

### 16.1 The mark is the origin label — and the marked issue IS the work item

> Rewritten 2026-08-20 (#1119, decision §15.29). The `claude-*` vocabulary and
> the shadow work item this replaces are decoded forever (§4's legacy table).

One label: a person applies **`task:origin:ad-hoc`** to an ordinary issue, and
that issue *becomes* the work item — no shadow `[claudinite-work]` issue is
filed for it, and the whole lifecycle (§4's statuses) plays out where the
person is already looking. The request state IS the queue state:

| shape | means |
|---|---|
| `task:origin:ad-hoc`, no status | marked, awaiting adoption — the exactly-once guard (§16.3) |
| + `task:status:waiting-for-executor` (or `blocked`) | adopted; a run is queued |
| + `task:status:running-executor` / `running-agent` | the run owns it |
| + `task:status:needs-human-approval` | a pull request is open, waiting on a person — the in-review state, with no separate label to mirror it |
| + `task:status:rejected` | refused and **disarmed** — standing on the still-open issue, because the run's verdict is not the issue's validity (§16.5) |

The mark is a label rather than a body syntax or a command comment for one
reason: it must be appliable from the issue page on a phone, and anything
richer is a form nobody fills in twice. It is also **write-gated by the
platform** — applying a label needs triage or write access — which is the
first half of the security story and the reason the rest can stay this small.
For an ad-hoc item the terminal statuses may stand on an **open** issue: the
issue's open/closed belongs to its author, the status to the run.

*Alternative — the shadow-item model this replaces (the marked issue holds the
conversation, a separate work item holds the state): two issues then tell one

input.title: A `task:status:done` terminal closes the issue it stands on, marked or filed
input.body:
Owner decision, reversing §16.1/§16.5's "a marked issue is never closed by its own run".

An ad-hoc request that converges `done` — the work is complete and nothing is left for anyone to act on — currently leaves the person's own issue **open**, wearing `task:status:done`. missingbulb/Shepherd#360 is the live case: the run posted its deliverable, the status landed, and the issue sat open with nothing for anyone to do on it.

**The requirement.** A terminal `task:status:done` closes the issue it stands on, whether that issue is a filed `[claudinite-work]` item or a marked ad-hoc one. Every other terminal is unchanged: a park is waiting on a person and stays open, and `task:status:rejected` still stands on the open marked issue, because a run's verdict is not the issue's validity.

**The three surfaces that carry the terminal**, all structurally identical and all to change together:

- `queue/converge-item.mjs` — `convergeOps`, the agentic session's own convergence (the surface Shepherd#360 hit).
- `queue/executor.mjs` — `close()`, the code-work path's `TASK_DONE` convergence.
- `tasks/task-janitor/queue-sweep.mjs` — an ended park whose pull request **merged**, which resolves to `TASK_DONE`. The unmerged half resolves to `TASK_OBSOLETE` and is unchanged.

Plus the places that state the old decision: `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §16.1 and §16.5, and the tests pinning it.

Closes #1489

missingbulb/Shepherd#360 ran, posted its deliverable, took `task:status:done` — and stayed **open**, with nothing on it for anyone to do. Two separate things had to be true for that, and both are here.

**A `done` terminal closes the issue it stands on.** §16.1/§16.5 said a marked issue is never closed by its own run: the status belongs to the run, the issue's open/closed to its author. That holds for every terminal but one. `done` is the outcome that means nothing is left for anyone to act on, so an issue left open under it is asking its author to come and agree with what the run already settled. It now closes either shape, at all three surfaces that carry the terminal — the session's `convergeOps`, the executor's code-work `close()`, and janitor rule G's *merged* half. Unchanged: a park waits on a person and stays open, and `task:status:rejected` still stands on the open marked issue, because a run's verdict is not the issue's validity. Each of the three has a contrast test pinning that half.

**Converge's membership test accepts an origin label.** It was gated on the machine block — the single artifact it exists to validate — so an item adopted before those delimiters existed read as "not a Claudinite work item". That is what actually happened on Shepherd#360: `converge-item.mjs` refused, the session performed the transition by hand, and the close was the step it dropped. An origin label is the independent signal — every item carries one for life, and applying it is platform-write-gated exactly as the block's adoption was. Any one of the three signals now suffices.

Without the second half the first would not have fired on the item that prompted it.

### What changed, by folder

```
packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/
  converge-item.mjs   the session's convergence: a done outcome always emits the
                      close op; membership accepts an origin label as a third signal
  executor.mjs        close() closes a marked issue on TASK_DONE, still returns
                      early for the rejected terminal

packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/task-janitor/
  queue-sweep.mjs     rule G closes on the RESOLUTION, not the item's shape:
                      merged closes completed, unmerged leaves a marked issue open

docs/tasks-dispatch/
  DESIGN.md           §16.1's sentence and shape table, §16.5's end table — the
                      reversal recorded where the old decision was stated
```

### Proof

Every behavioural change had its test written and watched fail first. Full suite: 2803 pass, 1 fail — `engine-pack-lane-shims`, which fails loudly by design in a shallow checkout and is unrelated. `check_the_work` and `check_the_world` are both 0 blocking.
